 On the show Craig Melvin Recalls Final Memories with Good Friend and NBC Announcer Dan Hicks
 The TODAY co-anchor remembered the legendary NBC Sports announcer after his death at 64 years old. Nov. 13, 2026, 9:50 AM EST / Source : TODAY Scott Stump
 Remembering Beloved NBC Sports Broadcaster Dan Hicks 03:16 Share Add TODAY to Google Craig Melvin sent his love to the “Hicks chicks” on TODAY and remembered his good friend as the sports world and NBC family mourned the loss of broadcaster Dan Hicks. 
 The 34-year veteran of NBC Sports was the voice of Olympic swimming and skiing, Notre Dame football and the PGA Tour. He died suddenly from an “acute illness” at 64 , his wife, ESPN “SportsCenter” anchor Hannah Storm, announced Nov. 12. 
 “He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable,” Storm wrote. 
 Craig and his wife, CBS Sports broadcaster Lindsay Czarniak , are close with the Hicks family. After reporting the news of Hicks’ death Nov. 12, Craig said they’ve become “part of our family.” 
 “Lindsay and I just had dinner with him,” he said. “He will be sorely missed.”
 He also shared a message about Hicks on TODAY Nov. 13. 
 “My wife Lindsay and I have been lucky enough to call Dan and Hannah our good friends for a number of years,” Craig said. “Saw him a few weeks ago at a charity event.” 
 Craig shared a photo on TODAY of the four of them together at the 2025 Rose Bowl in California. 
 Craig Melvin shares a photo of him and wife Lindsay Czarniak with Dan Hicks and Hannah Storm. Craig Melvin / TODAY “We are also sending our love to the Hicks chicks. That’s what Dan called his wife and girls — Hannah, Ellery and Riley,” Craig said. “We are of course thinking about you and keeping you in our thoughts and our prayers.” 
 Lindsay and Craig also posted a joint tribute to Hicks on Instagram Nov. 12, calling him, “simply the best.”
 “My biggest takeaway when I think of times with Hannah and Dan is the fact that he ALWAYS seemed genuinely happy, excited to see you and easy to talk to — just like he was so easy for all of us to listen to and watch in the most high stakes sports moments as a broadcaster,” they wrote.
 Tributes have poured in from around the sports world for Hicks, who was particularly known for memorable calls in golf and Olympic swimming. 
 “I can’t think of a big moment that Dan didn’t have the right call, the right energy, the right words,” NBC Sports broadcaster Mike Tirico said on TODAY Nov. 13. 
 Fellow sports broadcasting luminaries like ESPN’s Scott Van Pelt, NBC’s Jimmy Roberts and “Thursday Night Football’s” Al Michaels also sent their love to the Hicks family as they remembered their colleague. 
 “I’m just sad that he’s not here to hear all these folks saying kind things about him because he deserves it,” Roberts said on TODAY. 
 NBC Olympics swimming commentator Rowdy Gaines was particularly close with Hicks after calling eight Games alongside him. Hicks worked as a play-by-play announcer for 16 Olympics between the Summer and Winter Games, beginning in 1992. 
 Gaines held back tears as he remembered his friend on TODAY Nov. 13. 
 “Nobody ever had a bad word to say about Danny, and he never had a bad word to say about anybody else, and I think that just epitomizes the kind of person he was,” Gaines said.
 One of Hicks’ most memorable calls came during an electrifying comeback win by the U.S. team in the men’s 4x100 freestyle relay at the 2008 Olympics. The race is considered one of the greatest in Olympic swimming history. It also gave Michael Phelps his eighth gold medal in Beijing, the most any individual athlete has ever won in a single Olympics. Phelps shared a remembrance of Hicks on Nov. 12 on Instagram , calling the late broadcaster “a friend” and writing, “This one hurts.”
 “Phelps called me yesterday morning,” Gaines said on TODAY before pausing to collect himself. “He just said that (Hicks’) voice will never exit my head. We had this golden age of swimming. He knew more than anybody how to present that to the American audience. He was so prepared, and he was a guy that could do anything to let the audience come in and share those feelings.
 “It’s about caring for that person,” he added. “He made people care about them because he cared about them so much.” 
 Gaines called it “the greatest race in history, without a doubt.” Hicks’ voice reached a crescendo on the call as U.S. anchor Jason Lezak touched the wall first.
 “A lot of people think that’s me at the end because I’m normally the one yelling and screaming, but it was actually Dan’s voice that raised up like that at the end,” Gaines recalled. “It truly was an iconic race.”
